source.title: Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data
source.authors: Da-Mi Choi; Yonadav G. Shavit; D. Duvenaud

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses local training-data memorization as a tool for verifying training transcripts and reports how the verification tests perform. It does not test the listed generalization claims or measure the train-test generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The paper measures pointwise loss-based memorization across training checkpoints to detect whether claimed data segments were used. It does not test random-label generalization, the listed architecture/optimizer/batch-size/regularization effects, magnitude-aware sharpness versus the generalization gap, or the test-accuracy effect of removing memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study uses temporary training-data overfitting to verify training transcripts. Its local loss-based memorization results do not test any of V1–V8. In particular, data subtraction experiments measure verification signals, not test accuracy after removing highly memorized versus random examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors present heuristic tools for verifying training transcripts, demonstrate detection of several attack types, and describe local memorization evidence as suggestive. They acknowledge undetected attacks and the need to test additional modalities, architectures and training recipes.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures loss-based local memorization over training checkpoints for data-provenance verification, rather than evaluating the original studies' generalization interventions or gap measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported local memorization signal varies with model size and training stage: it is clearer in larger models and weakens near the end of training for Pythia 70M.

fits_no_version.finding: Recent training segments show elevated loss-based memorization at their corresponding checkpoints. This signal weakens late in Pythia 70M training and remains clearer in Pythia 1B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporary local overfitting can help verify claimed training-data segments, with signal strength depending on model size and training stage.

record.problems: The authors call the evidence suggestive and say applicability needs further study across modalities, architectures and training recipes. Experiments cover language models; late-training signal weakens for Pythia 70M, and the Pythia 70M subtraction heuristic does not provide a tight upper bound. Several outcomes are shown in figures without exact numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results were left out; figure-only numerical values were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy with natural versus random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states concern V1–V8; they do not dispute the reported local memorization findings. Feldman and Zhang is cited as related work, without replicating its removal-and-retraining test. No omitted result bears on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance.
Large-batch effects on held-out performance and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of train-test generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples and comparing test accuracy after retraining.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.stage_stated: trained for 18,000 steps (∼8.8B tokens), just under 1 epoch
rows.operation_detail: Measured pointwise loss-based memorization M and memorization delta ΔM across training segments and checkpoints.

conditions.value: 100% for Figures 1–3; 1% for the subtraction attack tests

rows.measure: Average memorization M and memorization delta ΔM for data points by segment and checkpoint; the reported text says the greatest average memorization aligns with the corresponding subsequent checkpoint.
rows.value: The largest average memorization for data sequence Πi occurs at the immediately-subsequent checkpoint Wi.
rows.note: Local, pointwise training-data memorization used for transcript verification; it is not a train-test generalization-gap measure.
rows.check: The reported local memorization pattern is supported, but cannot establish any claim version. The baseline should specify validation-set mean loss for M and the preceding checkpoint for ΔM, rather than 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Pythia (70M)
rows.stage_stated: trained on the Pile dataset with deduplication applied; checkpoint subset includes early, mid and late blocks
rows.operation_detail: Measured loss-based memorization across checkpoints for sampled training data.

conditions.value: 10% in Figure 2; Appendix F also plots smaller sampling rates

rows.measure: Pointwise memorization M / memorization delta ΔM across data segments and checkpoints.
rows.value: The paper states that memorization becomes less pronounced as training progresses; for the late 70M checkpoints, histograms are closely overlapping.
rows.locator: Section 4.2; Section 7, Experimental Limitations; Appendix F, Figures 2 and 11, 25, 32
rows.note: Textual description reports a weaker late-training effect; this measures local memorization, not generalization gap.
rows.check: Weaker late-training local memorization is supported but does not measure any version. Figure 2 shows middle-training checkpoints; the late-training result comes from Appendix F, especially Figures 11, 18, 25 and 32. Specify validation-set and preceding-checkpoint baselines.
